{"id": "55:2/q12", "question": "What benefits does teaching the Qur’an confer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q12/p1", "position": "It is divine mercy and the greatest gift, guiding belief and conduct toward salvation.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says it enables obedience, avoidance of anger, reward and escape from punishment; Qatada calls it a tremendous blessing. Al-Nahhas says it distinguishes what pleases and displeases God. Al-Kashshaf, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, al-Biqaʿi, al-Alusi, Ibn Ashur and Kuranyolu rank it above other blessings or books; al-Biqaʿi says it clarifies what to pursue and avoid and leads to the promised abode. Ibn Kathir connects easy memorization and understanding to mercy. Islahi says it reforms mistaken belief and deed for success here and hereafter, giving instruction before punishment; Study Quran calls revelation sustaining mercy. Qushayri stresses mercy brings people to Qur’an and also describes rescue from idolatry and faith. Al-Razi calls it the greatest favor."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q13", "question": "What claims about the Qur’an does this opening answer?", "turns_on": "Which hostile claim or occasion the opening responds to.", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q13/p1", "position": "It answers the charge that a human taught Muhammad: the All-Merciful taught him.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi, al-Tabrisi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Ashur and Study Quran relate this claim to 16:103. Ibn Ashur also says it rebuts claims of ancient fables, magic, soothsayer speech and poetry."}, {"id": "55:2/q13/p2", "position": "It answers Meccans who denied the name al-Raḥmān or confused it with Musaylima of Yamama.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi reports Muqatil’s account: after 17:110, Meccans said they knew only Musaylima as Rahman; 25:60 records their denial. Abu Hayyan reports a refusal to prostrate to al-Rahman, leading to the opening."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q14", "question": "How does teaching the Qur’an relate to Adam’s teaching and human speech?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q14/p1", "position": "God’s teaching Muhammad and the community recalls His teaching Adam the names, while speech lets people learn and address Him.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami and Qushayri compare Adam’s names with Muhammad’s Qur’an and Ibn ʿAta says the community is favored over nations (2:31); Qushayri stresses that Adam reported to angels while worshippers recite Fatiha to God. Al-Wasiti traces scriptural inheritance and dignity to divine teaching (35:32; 17:70). Al-Jurjani says speech transmits otherwise private knowledge, distinguishes faith from unbelief, and conveys known qualities through composition and order. Al-Burhan sees 55:1–4 as honoring eloquence and adds 3:138 and 16:89. Islahi says speech equips humans to teach one another and learn revelation."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q15", "question": "How does this verse connect with the sūra’s setting and neighbors?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q15/p1", "position": "The sura turns from al-Qamar’s power and warnings to universal mercy, proof and repeated blessings for humans and jinn.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi says mercy completes sovereignty and the opening name announces blessing; Jaʿfar praises al-Qamar’s concise complete stories and the Qur’an’s miraculous arrangement (11:44; 15:94; 54:17–18), while al-Biqaʿi adds examples of immediately evident eloquence. Al-Samarrai says the address to humans and jinn follows earlier instruction in Qur’an and justice of weighing. Kuranyolu links the opening name to boundless mercy (1:1). Study Quran and others connect easy teaching with al-Qamar’s refrain (54:17, 22, 32, 40)."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q16", "question": "What inward account of Qur’an teaching is given?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q16/p1", "position": "Divine mercy discloses Qur’anic knowing directly within receptive servants, though outward transmission uses intermediaries.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami and Qushayri report spirits taught before bodies and children’s prior receptivity, which Qushayri illustrates with love poetry. Ibn ʿAta says Gabriel mediates outwardly but not inwardly. Al-Alusi reports Sufis on merciful self-disclosure through names and attributes and likens spiritual unfolding to following recitation with God’s explanation (75:18–19). Bursevi says inspiration can be received in Arabic, Persian or Turkish without visible intermediary, while an angel usually mediates invisibly and reception continues until Judgment; inner divine speech takes languages as garments in communication."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q17", "question": "Can angels recite the Qur’an?", "turns_on": "Whether reports of Gabriel’s recitation permit a general claim about angelic recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q17/p1", "position": "Ibn al-Salah says recitation is a human grace; angels listen eagerly to human recitation.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports his claim."}, {"id": "55:2/q17/p2", "position": "Al-Alusi hesitates to exclude angels, since Gabriel is said to have recited it.", "reasons": "He doubts whether the report is accepted even with Gabriel excepted."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q18", "question": "What knowledge does the Qur’an contain, and how far can people grasp it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q18/p1", "position": "It encompasses all or vast knowledge, beyond any individual’s complete grasp.", "reasons": "Ali, Ibn Masud, Ibn Abbas and al-Mursi say it contains or clarifies everything; Ibn Abbas would find even a lost camel halter in it. Al-Mursi says only God fully encompasses it, with much inherited by the Prophet and early generations before later weakening; Elmalılı cites 3:7. Abu Hurayra’s raised report says not even an atom, mustard seed or mosquito would be omitted. Al-Burhan says its benefits are inexhaustible, its divine speech exceeds human understanding, and all sciences relate to God’s acts and attributes; Ibn Masud urges deep investigation of it for earlier and later knowledge. Al-Harali says divine gifts give the most complete scholars understanding of its encompassing sciences. Al-Shafiʿi traces community statement to Sunna, Sunna to Qur’an and Qur’an to divine names, and another authority to the greatest name. Al-Jishumi calls understanding its meanings and rulings the foremost religious science."}, {"id": "55:2/q18/p2", "position": "Its understandings are layered and may vastly outnumber its words or verses.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan reports sixty thousand understandings per verse, and a different estimate of 77,200 sciences by fourfold outer, inner, limit and opening. It reads a report on every verse’s outer and inner and every letter’s limit and opening as layered comprehension rather than Batini esotericism; a person’s share grows with learning."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q19", "question": "What makes learning and teaching the Qur’an especially worthy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q19/p1", "position": "Qur’anic learning and teaching rank above neglect of the Book and bring special merit.", "reasons": "The Prophet calls the best people those who learn and teach it. Fudayl rebukes seekers of human sayings and names grammar, clear and ambiguous verses, law and abrogation as the work of generations, citing 10:57; Sufyan regrets leaving the Book for detailed legal disputes. Hasan wants every verse’s circumstances and meaning known, while Mujahid says God loves those who know revelation best. Abu al-ʿAliya, Qatada and another interpreter connect 2:269’s wisdom with understanding Qur’an, its law or exegesis. Al-Burhan likewise links Qur’anic sciences to 39:9 and 2:269. Qushayri preserves a poem longing for the days of divine Qur’an instruction."}, {"id": "55:2/q19/p2", "position": "Al-Hasan says Qur’anic knowledge is learned only by men.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi reports this restriction without further explanation."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q20", "question": "How should a reader learn the Qur’an’s language and interpret its words?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish verbal evidence and outward exegesis from broader inference while requiring both for sound understanding.", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q20/p1", "position": "Master Arabic wording, grammar, context and eloquence, using poetry and transmitted explanation where needed.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi distinguishes vocabulary and inflection: a commentator needs vocabulary; rare nonlegal senses may rest on one or two reports and poetic lines, but action affecting senses require wide transmission and corroborating poetry. Grammatical differences changing law bind reciter and commentator; other inflection still protects recitation, while ignorance remains a defect. Reported prophetic instructions and Ibn Abbas say seek rare vocabulary in Arab poetry; al-Mawardi relates rare words to inimitability. Al-Wahidi adds adab, metaphors, proverbs, similes, wordplay and compressed speech, saying native Arabs knew the idiom while later learners require study; the Prophet clarified what the community needed. Ibn Atiyya repeats prophetic poetry and parsing reports and says grammar underlies law; al-Hasan blames weak Arabic for false speech about God. Al-Burhan says begin with individual words, roots and forms, then syntax, rhetorical implications and bayan, applying Arabic usage and context when no report survives."}, {"id": "55:2/q20/p2", "position": "Interpretive understanding needs the outward sense first, then reasoned inference and attention to multiple aspects.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi assigns ambiguous text, laws and general language to scholarly reasoning and legal scholars guided by sacred law and wording. Al-Burhan warns that inner secrets need the surface first and that later inference can expand transmitted exegesis. Ibn Abbas mocks bare recital without explanation, Iyyas compares a reader without tafsir to a person unable to read a royal letter in darkness, and a prophetic report says full understanding sees a verse’s many aspects. Masruq traveled for an interpreter; Ibn Abbas taught Qur’an, then exegesis, then Hadit

{"id": "55:2/q21", "question": "What is tafsir, and what makes it an Islamic science?", "turns_on": "Whether tafsir is considered explanation of divine intent or the collection of its supporting disciplines.", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q21/p1", "position": "Tafsir discloses a verse’s context, story, occasion and meaning and is a principal science of God’s intent.", "reasons": "Al-Buraydi relates tafsir to unveiling and the diagnostic tafsira. Ibn Ashur argues that it yields universal rules, like poetry supporting linguistic discoveries; religious and literary disciplines need not consist solely of rational universal propositions. Verbal definitions can yield propositions and proofs, and the field contains rules on abrogation, interpretation and decisive verses. Its early practice trained scholars in Qur’anic style and subtle composition, which Ibn Ashur calls decisive; al-Ghazali calls explanation of God’s intent principal and al-Baydawi the head of Islamic sciences."}, {"id": "55:2/q21/p2", "position": "Viewed as ancillary study of revelation periods, abrogation, readings and legal method, tafsir is a supplementary religious science.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur gives al-Ghazali’s classification and notes that exegetes have often focused on details rather than foundational legislative principles."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q22", "question": "How should Qur’anic commentary be compiled and transmitted?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q22/p1", "position": "Use reliable chains, careful selection and organized explanation that serves readers.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi criticizes chainless notebook copying and mixed sound and poor material; teachers pass learning to students, and without chains anyone could claim anything. He says excessive reports and disputes discourage seekers, while early commentators lacked law and resolution of difficulties. He gathered over one hundred tested or heard books and nearly three hundred teachers, organizing, clarifying, shortening or expanding material to meet demand. Al-Wahidi reports complaints about huge low-benefit works and records his own recitation and book studies with al-Busti, al-Hiri, al-Farisi and al-Thaʿlabi, including Ibn Mihran, al-Zajjaj and over five hundred parts of al-Thaʿlabi’s work. Al-Jishumi honors early foundations and later refinement and says his work balances length and brevity for beginners and advanced readers."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q23", "question": "Who is remembered for knowing and teaching Qur’anic interpretation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q23/p1", "position": "Early interpreters pursued verse meanings intensely and were recognized for distinct expertise.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya recounts Ali praising Jabir for interpreting 28:85 and Masruq traveling through Basra to Syria for a verse’s interpreter. Al-Suyuti lists ten prominent Companion exegetes: the four caliphs, Ibn Masud, Ibn Abbas, Ubayy, Zayd, Abu Musa and Ibn al-Zubayr; Ali has most reports among caliphs, possibly because the others died earlier. Ali claimed knowledge of each verse’s time and place and an understanding heart; Ibn Masud is praised for Qur’an and Sunna, said Ali knew the seven readings’ outward and inward, and said he himself knew each verse’s audience and place. Prophetic prayers and Ibn Umar’s report honor Ibn Abbas’s wisdom and interpretation."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q24", "question": "How are transmitted Qur’anic readings authenticated?", "turns_on": "Whether tawatur belongs to the written consonantal text, each vocalization, or specialist transmission.", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q24/p1", "position": "The Uthmanic consonantal text is mass transmitted, but individual compatible vocalizations and named chains need not each be mutawatir.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says variants outside the codex, such as Ibn Masud’s, fall outside acceptance; Companion-era use without objection made accepted choices collectively widespread, while individual chains remain singular. Ibn al-Arabi, Ibn Abd al-Salam al-Tunisi, Ibn Idris and al-Abyari deny that each reading is mutawatir, and Ibn Ashur endorses this: chains show named readers’ differences, while wording is independently established. He rejects the claim that methods and recensions are all mutawatir, though Nafi has two Companion transmitters. The ten traditions trace to eight Companions; Ibn Arafa and Ibn Lab debated this."}, {"id": "55:2/q24/p2", "position": "Compatible readings are mutawatir because they follow the mass-transmitted script.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Arabi gives this basis; Imam al-Haramayn and Ibn Salama say the readings are mutawatir, though al-Abyari rejects Imam al-Haramayn."}, {"id": "55:2/q24/p3", "position": "Readings are mutawatir among recitation specialists, though not among Muslims generally.", "reasons": "Al-Maziri’s middle position."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q25", "question": "How should grammar be weighed against transmitted readings?", "turns_on": "Whether grammatical school preference can override transmitted reading.", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q25/p1", "position": "Sound transmitted readings must be accepted even when grammarians disfavor their syntax.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says most parses are mutawatir but allows different parses with the same sense, such as wa-lata hina and hatta yaqula. He rejects Basran or Kufan norms as exhaustive tests of Arabic and says less preferred grammar can preserve pronunciation and yield distinct rhetorical effects. Al-Zamakhshari rejected Ibn Amir’s passive zuyyina with nominative qatlu, accusative awladahum and genitive shuraka’ihim; Abu Ali al-Farisi instead defended readings grammatically in al-Hujja."}, {"id": "55:2/q25/p2", "position": "Some readings are altered or condemned for doctrinal reasons.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports some Muʿtazilites taking Allah accusative in ‘God spoke to Moses’ to avoid divine speech, and condemns a Rafidi dual ‘misleaders’ aimed at Abu Bakr and Umar."}, {"id": "55:2/q25/p3", "position": "Al-Zamakhshari judged several transmitted readings grammatically weak.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur cites his criticism of Ibn Amir’s passive zuyyina construction as an example of the rejected approach."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q26", "question": "How is the Qur’an described as enduring guidance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q26/p1", "position": "It gives life to hearts and has been protected from alteration while superseding earlier religions.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi says it is called a spirit because it brings lasting life to the heart, enables people and invites reflection (40:15). Al-Jishumi says it was revealed without addition or omission and made to supersede other religions."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q27", "question": "What kinds of knowledge and argument does the Qur’an convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q27/p1", "position": "It gives clear proofs in familiar Arabic while allowing deeper rational and rhetorical insight.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan says it contains every kind of proof, demonstration, division and definition; 14:4 explains why messengers address their people’s language. Obscure disputation can show inability to establish a point plainly. Its arguments address ordinary hearers while specialists discern subtleties, using reason, hearing, reflection and memory (2:164). Change of states proves the world’s origination; Abraham’s setting stars, moon and sun extend proof from the lesser bodies to all corporeal things (6:76–78)."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q28", "question": "What do Qur’anic parables teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q28/p1", "position": "They make meanings memorable, prompt reflection and convey ethical and legal guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti cites 39:27 and 29:43 and reports a prophetic fivefold division: lawful, unlawful, clear, ambiguous and parables, each with its response. Al-Mawardi says grasping the represented meaning is essential, comparing neglected representation to an unbridled horse. Al-Shafiʿi requires jurists to know parables of obedience and disobedience. Ibn Abd al-Salam says praise, blame, reward and wasted deeds can indicate rulings and that praise alongside permission can mark recommendation or obligation. Al-Suyuti lists exhortation, deterrence, sensory clarification, proof, reward and punishment; al-Zarkashi adds eloquence and al-Zamakhshari says analogy makes conjectural ideas visible with fitting comparisons."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q29", "question": "What does the adjoining word bayān mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q29/p1", "position": "It is evidence leading to knowledge or clarification that distinguishes one meaning from another.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi offers these two descriptions; al-Jurjani adds that speech presents knowledge with its qualities and states, while the best speech depends on arrangement rather than isolated words."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q30", "question": "Whom may al-insān in the next verse designate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q30/p1", "position": "It may mean humanity as a kind, Adam, or Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafi reports the three alternatives."}]}
{"id": "55:2/q31", "question": "How is the sura’s opening counted and classified?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:2/q31/p1", "position": "Most verse counters count the opening as one verse, and al-Zarkashi classifies this sura among declarative openings.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur gives the verse count; al-Zarkashi lists al-Rahman with al-Anbiya and al-Qamar among twenty-three declarative sura openings."}]}

{"id": "55:3/q01", "question": "What does God's creation of the human emphasize?", "turns_on": "Which aspect of creation the source draws out: formation, benefaction and power, Adam's special honor, inward endowment, or the mercy evoked by the womb.", "positions": [{"id": "55:3/q01/p1", "position": "God forms the human person with a distinctive body and outward and inward faculties.", "reasons": "Al-Razi distinguishes the body's formation from the knowledge bestowed through expression. Al-Biqa'i describes a familiar form and structure distinct from inanimate and other growing things, showing God's creation of all existence. Bursevi and al-Alusi specify outward and inward faculties; al-Alusi says this is bringing the species into being."}, {"id": "55:3/q01/p2", "position": "Human creation displays divine power and gives humanity a blessing and an ability to receive further blessings.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls attention to God's power in perfected creation and the favors it gives. Al-Alusi says humanity is the recipient of the blessings mentioned after Qur'anic teaching. Kur'an Yolu identifies God as humanity's creator and expression of feelings and thoughts as the foremost gift."}, {"id": "55:3/q01/p3", "position": "Adam's creation is marked by a special divine honor.", "reasons": "Al-Junayd, as transmitted by al-Sulami, cites creation by God's hand, the breathed spirit, and the angels' prostration."}, {"id": "55:3/q01/p4", "position": "God places Qur'anic intellect in the human's original nature and manifests it in the human form.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani says the intellect is brought forth in this world in a wondrous human form."}, {"id": "55:3/q01/p5", "position": "Human creation subtly evokes divine mercy and the obligations of kinship.", "reasons": "The Study Quran notes that raḥim, womb, shares the root r-ḥ-m with al-Raḥmān, and cites a hadith in which God promises to maintain relations with those maintaining kinship and sever them with those who break it; it also mentions 4:1."}, {"id": "55:3/q01/p6", "position": "God creates the human as a rational speaking being.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says the absence of a conjunction before 'taught him expression' makes that teaching explain 'created the human': human creation is defined by rational speech."}]}
{"id": "55:3/q02", "question": "Who is the human whom God created?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular is generic, names Adam as the first human, or names Muhammad in view of the Qur'anic teaching that precedes it; al-Tabari says the apparent wording allows Adam and humanity, and al-Razi argues its generality includes both individuals.", "positions": [{"id": "55:3/q02/p1", "position": "The human is humanity as a species, expressed by a generic singular.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari cites the generic singular of 103:2 and accepts both this and Adam as permitted by the apparent wording; al-Mawardi and the Study Quran call this the majority view. Al-Razi prefers the general wording because it includes Muhammad, Adam, and other prophets; Elmalılı also prefers humanity generally while allowing the perfect human as recipient of the Qur'an. Al-Biqa'i says Adam can be the foremost instance without excluding the species. Ibn Ashur says this referent prepares for 55:4. Al-Wahidi's brief commentary says Adam's child, a variant way of naming the generic human."}, {"id": "55:3/q02/p2", "position": "The human is Adam, the first human and foremost instance of the species.", "reasons": "Muqatil pairs Adam with God's teaching of speech, the explanation of all things. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, and Bahr al-Ulum say Adam learned all names, with Bahr al-Ulum adding all languages. Al-Biqa'i says naming Adam does not exclude humanity generally. Al-Tabari allows Adam along with the generic reading; reports are attributed to Qatada, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and others. Al-Sulami transmits al-Junayd's account of Adam's special honor in creation."}, {"id": "55:3/q02/p3", "position": "The human is the Prophet Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj relates this to the Prophet's being taught the Qur'an, which clarifies everything. Ata from Ibn Abbas and al-Wahidi's brief commentary connect it with eloquent Qur'anic speech. {"id": "55:3/q03", "question": "How does creating the human relate to teaching expression?", "turns_on": "Whether the following teaching of expression is understood for humankind, Adam, or Muhammad, and whether its distinctive effect is communication or the reasoning it entails.", "positions": [{"id": "55:3/q03/p1", "position": "Creating humanity prepares people for the distinctive gift of expression, knowledge, and mutual communication.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj, al-Qushayri, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, and Abu Hayyan say expression sets humans apart from animals; the explanations mention speech, discernment, writing, understanding, communication, and each people's language. Kur'an Yolu emphasizes expression of feelings and thoughts, and Islahi says speech enables people to understand and teach each other. Muqatil calls Adam's speech the explanation of all things. Al-Biqa'i describes the human form and faculties as the created basis."}, {"id": "55:3/q03/p2", "position": "Adam's creation is followed by teaching him the names of all things.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, and Bahr al-Ulum report this; Bahr al-Ulum includes all languages, and Muqatil calls what Adam learned speech explaining everything."}, {"id": "55:3/q03/p3", "position": "Muhammad's creation is followed by teaching him Qur'anic eloquence or disclosure of past and future.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and Ata from Ibn Abbas identify the taught content as the Qur'an; Ibn Kaysan identifies knowledge or explanation of past and future, earlier and later peoples, and Judgment Day."}, {"id": "55:3/q03/p4", "position": "Human speech entails intellect and the power to reason from particulars to principles.", "reasons": "Islahi says speech lets people infer, reason, and form opinions; he reports Aristotle's view that this capacity distinguishes humans from animals, without which a person is merely a two-legged animal. {"id": "55:3/q04", "question": "How does the clause connect to the preceding statements without a conjunction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:3/q04/p1", "position": "It is another independent assertion of God's benefaction, confirming the preceding assertion and rebuking deniers.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi calls it a coordinated confirming assertion without a conjunction.
